title: One chemical reaction helps feed nearly half of humanity
body: Nitrogen makes up most of the air, but plants can’t use it directly because the two atoms in N₂ are held together by an extremely strong triple bond. The Haber–Bosch process, developed in Germany around 1909 to 1913, forces nitrogen and hydrogen together over an iron catalyst to make ammonia for fertiliser. It is estimated that the food grown with that fertiliser supports nearly half the world’s population.

slides.question: Haber–Bosch plants turn nitrogen and hydrogen into ammonia. What share of the gas reacts in a single pass?
slides.explanation: Only about 15% per pass, even at around 500 °C and roughly 200 times atmospheric pressure, so the leftover nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled through again.

slides.heading: Heat, pressure, iron
slides.text: Classic plants run at around 500 °C and roughly 200 times atmospheric pressure. Only about 15% converts per pass, so leftover gas is recycled.

steps.label: Nitrogen from the air is mixed with hydrogen
Ammonia is drawn off; leftover gas recycles

slides.heading: Drop by drop
slides.text: Fritz Haber’s 1909 lab demonstration made ammonia from air at about 125 ml per hour. By 1914 a BASF plant was making 20 tonnes a day.

slides.heading: The hidden cost
slides.text: Ammonia production uses roughly 1–2% of global energy. It also let Germany make explosives in World War I despite being cut off from imported nitrates.
